title.en: The Serpent and the Forbidden Knowledge

text.en: Within the team of creators, a small group, the “serpent” of the story, wanted the humans to know the truth. They came to the woman and questioned the ban: had the Elohim really said that nothing in the garden was to be eaten?

The woman answered that they were free to learn from everything around them. Only the scientific knowledge kept at the centre of the garden was forbidden: the creators had said that they were not even to touch it, or they would die.

The group told the two young people, almost adults by now, that they would not die. They could pursue scientific studies; their eyes would be opened, and they would be as strong as their creators, like the Elohim themselves.
The woman judged this knowledge good, attractive, and worth having for the understanding it gave, and she took it up. The man was with her, and he took it up too.

Their eyes were opened. They understood that they too could become creators, and they resented their fathers for having forbidden them to touch the scientific books, as if they were dangerous laboratory animals. In the verse’s image, they saw that they were naked and made themselves belts of fig leaves.

The Messages quote this dialogue in abridged form, ending on the promise “ye shall be as gods”, and explain it at once. Among the scientists of the team that created the first humans, a few who deeply loved their little men, their “creatures”, wanted to give them a complete education and make them scientists like themselves. They told these young people, who were almost adults, that they could pursue scientific studies and would be as strong as their creators.
When the Messages come to the serpent’s sentence they say who the serpent was: “that small group of creators who had wanted to teach Adam and Eve the truth”.

In his own commentary, *Let’s Welcome the Extraterrestrials*, Raël names the leader of this group Lucifer, “light bearer”. The dictated Messages give the group no leader and no name; this is the author’s opinion, cited as such, not canon.
*Nachash* is the ordinary Hebrew word for a snake. The serpent is called *arum*, “shrewd”, a sound-play on *arummim*, “naked”, in 2:25; the two words sound alike but come from different roots.

The Messages explain the forbidden tree when they quote the ban of 2:16–17: “you may learn everything you want, read all the books we have here at your disposal, but do not touch the scientific books or you will die.” The man created in this team was the most intelligent, so the creators confined him “in ignorance of the great scientific secrets while being educated, so that his intelligence could be measured”, in order that the created would not surpass the creator.
“Knowing good and bad” is read by many scholars as a merism, a pair of opposites standing for knowledge as a whole; others take it as moral discernment or as the capacity to decide for oneself.
The Messages read the forbidden knowledge as science: their gloss of the ban turns the tree into “the scientific books”.

Glossing the “wickedness” of Genesis 6:5, the Messages later define the pair from the side of the distant planet’s authorities: “Good, for them, was that man should remain a primitive being vegetating on Earth. Evil was that he should want to make progress, risking one day being in a position to rejoin his creators.”

The woman’s answer differs from the ban of 2:17. She adds “you shall not touch it”, and she softens “you shall surely die” to “lest you die”. The Messages’ paraphrase of the ban, which glosses 2:17, also speaks of touching: “do not touch the scientific books”.

Rabbinic tradition also doubts that the fence was hers. In *Avot de-Rabbi Natan* (version A, chapter 1) it is Adam who adds “you shall not touch it” when he passes the command on to her, and the serpent then pushes her against the tree to show that touching it does not kill.

One Wheel of Heaven reading therefore takes her “touch” as an echo of the creators’ own wording of the ban, so that she would not have added the fence herself. The match exists only in the Messages’ French and English; Genesis gives the ban of 2:17 without it, and the Messages do not comment on her words.

The serpent’s promise, *ke-elohim*, can be read “like God” or “like gods”. The Greek Septuagint and the King James Version have the plural, “as gods”, and so does the Messages’ quotation; the Wheel of Heaven translation reads “like the Elohim”.
In the Messages the promise is concrete: the humans could study the sciences and become “as strong as their creators”.

The Messages quote verse 7, “And the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked”, and say what was understood: “Then they understood that they too could become creators, and they resented their fathers for having forbidden them to touch the scientific books, thus regarding them as dangerous laboratory animals.”
Verse 7 repeats the verb of the serpent’s promise in verse 5, “your eyes will be opened” (*paqach*). Within the story, the first of the serpent’s predictions comes true in the same words.

The Messages say nothing of the fig leaves. Their comment follows directly on the words “they knew that they were naked”, so in their reading the new awareness of nakedness stands for the discovery that the humans too could become creators.

The chapter never uses the word “sin”; in Genesis the word (*chattat*) first appears at 4:7. The doctrine of a “Fall” and of original sin was developed in Christian theology, above all by Augustine, building on Paul (Romans 5:12–21). Some Jewish writings of the late Second Temple period lament the consequences of Adam’s act for his descendants (4 Ezra 7:118), but rabbinic Judaism did not make the episode a doctrine of inherited guilt.
The Messages tell the episode without any language of sin: in their account the humans learned the truth from a few creators who “deeply loved” them.
Elsewhere the Messages name the doctrine once, speaking of “those who make people believe in original sin and make a man a culprit”.
When the creators were heard walking about in the garden in the evening breeze, the man and the woman hid from them among the trees.
The creators called to the man. He answered that he had hidden out of fear because he was naked: the knowledge the two had gained made them see themselves differently in front of their makers.

The questions traced the knowledge to its source. The man pointed to the woman, and beyond her to the one who had given her to him; the woman pointed to the serpent. In the Messages’ terms, the trail led to the small group of creators who had taught them.
The Messages do not comment on this passage; what follows is a Wheel of Heaven reading.

In this Reading the Hebrew *YHWH-Elohim* is rendered as the creators. The dictated Messages do give their speaker’s name, “My name is Yahweh and I am the president of the council of the eternals” (ETTMTTP 2:50), but they do not identify him with the *YHWH-Elohim* of this scene.

The scene is a questioning in three steps: “Where are you?” (*ayekka*), “Who told you that you were naked?”, and “What is this you have done?”. Each answer passes the responsibility on: the man to the woman and to the one who gave her to him, the woman to the serpent.
Read with the Messages, the question “Who told you?” has a literal answer. A small group of creators had told the humans that they could study the sciences and become like their makers.

The woman says “the serpent deceived me” (*hishiani*). Within the story, however, what the serpent promised comes true: the eyes are opened (3:7), and the creators themselves say that the human has become “like one of us” (3:22). The death threatened “on the day” of eating does not follow; Adam lives on to 930 years (5:5). James Barr, Regius Professor of Hebrew at Oxford from 1978 to 1989, argued in *The Garden of Eden and the Hope of Immortality* (1992) that the story tells how humans lost the chance of immortality, not how sin entered the world.

This fits the Messages’ description of the serpent as creators “who had wanted to teach Adam and Eve the truth”. On this reading, the deception the woman names is her defence under questioning; the narrator calls the serpent shrewd but never calls its words a lie.

The small group of creators who had taught the humans was condemned by the government of the original planet to live on Earth in exile, while the other creators had to stop their experiments and leave the Earth. In the verse’s image, the serpent is to go on its belly and eat dust all its days.

Enmity was decreed between the serpent and the woman, and between their offspring, each striking at the other. The Messages do not quote this verse, and in their sequel the exiles stay close to humankind: they take wives among the daughters of men.

The Messages quote the curse on the serpent, “upon thy belly shalt thou go, and dust shalt thou eat all the days of thy life”, and explain it: the “serpent”, “that small group of creators who had wanted to teach Adam and Eve the truth”, “was condemned by the government of the original planet to live on Earth in exile, while the other creators had to stop their experiments and leave the Earth.”

The Messages themselves make a second link. Speaking of “the creators banished at the beginning”, who hid in bases under the oceans, they quote Isaiah 27:1 on Leviathan, “the fleeing serpent” (French « le serpent fuyard »). The Wheel of Heaven reading takes this serpent vocabulary, the *nachash* of this chapter and the Leviathan of Isaiah, as the way the tradition remembered the exiled group, judged passage by passage rather than for every serpent in the Bible. The reading rests on the Messages’ identification, not on any etymology of the word.

Of the three addressed in verses 14–19, only the serpent hears “cursed are you” (*arur attah*). For the man it is the ground that is cursed “because of you” (3:17), and the woman is not cursed at all. Mainstream commentators also read verse 14 as an etiology, a story explaining why snakes move on their bellies.
The Messages quote verse 14 but not verse 15; what follows on the enmity is a Wheel of Heaven reading.

The verb of verse 15 (*shuf*, strike or crush) is used for both sides: the woman’s offspring strikes the serpent’s head, and the serpent strikes its heel. From Irenaeus in the second century, Christian tradition read the verse as the first announcement of a redeemer, later called the “protoevangelium”; in the Latin West the Vulgate’s *ipsa conteret*, “she shall crush”, turned that reading toward Mary. In the Hebrew the pronoun *hu* and its verb are masculine, agreeing with *zera*, “offspring”.

In the Messages’ sequel the exiled creators, “who remained under military surveillance”, urged the men to bring them food to show that the beings they had created “would never turn against their fathers”, and they took the most beautiful daughters of men as wives.

One Wheel of Heaven reading takes the enmity as the separation the authorities of the original planet wanted to impose between the exiles and the humans, not as a hostility that arose between them. Nothing in the canon states this.

To the woman the verse announces hardship and many pregnancies, and a longing for her husband, who would rule over her. These are the terms of life for a humanity that would now raise its children without the creators’ help.

To the man it announces that the ground would give its food only to hard work, among thorns and thistles, until he returned to the dust he was made from. Outside the garden the humans would feed themselves by their own labour, and their lives would stay short.
The man named his woman Chavvah (Eve), “living”, for she was to be the mother of all who live: the first mother of a humanity that would now continue on its own.
The Messages do not comment on this passage; what follows is a Wheel of Heaven reading.

The woman’s hardship in bearing children (*itsavon*, *etsev*) and the man’s hardship in working the ground (*itsavon*, 3:17) use the same Hebrew root. Carol Meyers, archaeologist and biblical scholar at Duke University, reads verse 16 in *Discovering Eve* (1988) against the demands of farming life in the Israelite highlands: more toil and more pregnancies.

From this speech the Messages quote only the sentence on the serpent, and they describe the humans’ new condition in practical terms: the creators gave them “rudimentary means of survival, enough to manage on their own without contact with them”. Read in that light, verses 16–19 describe the conditions of life without the creators’ care.
“You are dust, and to dust you shall return” uses *afar*, the dust of 2:7 from which the human was formed.

In the Messages, humans were not made long-lived: “Men’s lives are very short”, and the means of prolonging them, the “tree of life”, is what the creators withhold at 3:22. On this reading, verse 19 states a mortality the humans already had.

A passage in “The Keys”, the closing chapter of *Extraterrestrials Took Me to Their Planet*, echoes this verse: “You were only matter, dust, and the Elohim made of you living beings capable of dominating matter, in their image, and you will become matter again, dust, and they will make you live again, as they created you, scientifically.” “The Keys” is Raël’s own writing, not dictated text; the passage is cited as the author’s opinion, not as the Messages’ reading.

*Chavvah* is linked by the verse to *chai*, “living”. The Greek Septuagint translates the name here as *Zoe* (Ζωή), “Life”, and first transliterates it at 4:1 (Εὕα); the English “Eve” comes from that Greek form through the Latin *Eva*, the form of the Old Latin and of the New Testament (the Vulgate of Genesis has *Hava*, in the Clementine edition *Heva*). The Messages use the names Adam and Eve.
The creators made tunics of skin for the man and the woman and clothed them: part of the rudimentary means of survival they gave the two, enough to manage on their own without contact with them.

The Messages quote the verse, “Unto the man also and to his wife did Elohim make coats of skins, and clothed them”, and explain: “The creators gave them rudimentary means of survival, enough to manage on their own without contact with them. The Bible has here preserved a phrase almost intact from the original document.”
The tunics of hide replace the improvised fig-leaf belts of verse 7. The text does not say where the skins came from.
In the Messages’ account the gesture is provision before parting: the humans are equipped to live without their makers.

title.en: The Tree of Life and the Expulsion

text.en: The human had become like one of the creators, through science. Now he had to be kept from the “tree of life”, the scientific means of prolonging life for a very long time: with lives that long, humans would very quickly become the creators’ equals.
So the man was sent away from the garden to work the ground he had been taken from, and to live from then on without contact with his creators.

At the entrance to the creators’ residence, on the east side of the garden, military personnel with disintegrating atomic weapons were posted to stop the humans from coming to steal further scientific knowledge.
The Messages quote verse 22, “Behold, the man is become as one of us (…). And now, lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever.”

The project’s English text of the Messages, which gives the quotation in King James wording, has only an ellipsis after “as one of us”. At that point the French original has the words *grâce à la science*, “thanks to science”, before its own ellipsis, which leaves out “knowing good and bad”. The phrase is the Messages’ gloss set inside the quotation; it is not in the Hebrew.

“Like one of us” is the second time Genesis has the divine speaker use the plural, after 1:26 (and before 11:7). Commentators explain it as speech to a heavenly court, as a plural of majesty, or as deliberation.
Read with the Messages, the “us” are the Elohim themselves, and the man has become like one of them by acquiring their science.

The Messages explain the tree of life as longevity: “Men’s lives are very short, and there is a scientific means of prolonging them for a very long time.” A scientist who studies all his life has enough knowledge to make interesting discoveries only when he grows old, hence the slowness of human progress. “If men could live ten times longer, they would make a gigantic scientific leap. If from the start they had been able to live so long, they would very quickly have become our equals, because their faculties are slightly superior to ours.”

The same paragraph goes on to the people of Israel. At one of the competitions among the teams of creators, they were “chosen by the scientific jury as the most successful terrestrial humanoid type in terms of intelligence and genius”, and the Messages give this as the origin of Israel’s understanding of itself as the chosen people: “it was the people chosen by the teams of creators gathered to judge their works.”

Wheel of Heaven records this clause as the canon’s account of a self-understanding, not as a ranking the corpus endorses, and makes no claim of biological superiority or individual worth. The election of Israel in the Hebrew Bible is a covenant theme in its own terms: Deuteronomy 7:6–8 grounds it in divine love and in the oath sworn to the fathers, not in Israel’s numbers.

Elsewhere the Messages say that the Elohim themselves live ten times longer than humans “thanks to a small surgical intervention”, which they identify with the biblical “tree of life”. Moses and Elijah, seen at the Transfiguration, are still alive thanks to it, and “Immortality is a scientific reality, even if it does not correspond to the idea that man makes of it.”

The tree was later granted to the chiefs of the first men, which the Messages give as the reason for the long lives of Genesis 5: Adam nine hundred and thirty years, Seth nine hundred and twelve. “Longevity is not hereditary”, and the children of men did not automatically benefit from it.

Other Near Eastern stories also tie lost immortality to a plant or a food. In the *Epic of Gilgamesh* (tablet XI) a snake steals the plant of rejuvenation; in the myth of Adapa, the hero, on the advice of the god Ea, refuses the bread and water of life offered by the god Anu.

The Messages quote verse 24, “So he drove out the man; and he placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life”, and explain it: “Military personnel possessing disintegrating atomic weapons were placed at the entrance to the creators’ residence in order to prevent man from coming to steal further scientific knowledge.”

In Hebrew the *keruvim* are winged composite guardians, comparable to the figures that flank palace and temple gateways in Mesopotamian art, and the “flaming blade” is one that “turns itself” (*mithappechet*).

The disclosure and the exile open a conflict between the government of the original planet and the exiled creators that the Messages follow through the next chapters: the exiles under military surveillance (Genesis 4), their marriages with the daughters of men (Genesis 6), and the Flood.
